rows.new_version_name: Qur'anic root: shirkah / partners (Qur'an 38:24 and 4:12)
rows.what_changed: The Qur'an speaks of partners. One verse (38:24) says that many partners wrong each other, except those who believe and do good, and that such people are few. A commentary on that verse says it is not unusual for partners to compromise each other's rights, so great caution is needed. Another verse (4:12) says that if they are more than one, they all share one third of the estate. A report in the collection of Abu Dawud has God say that He is the third of two partners as long as neither cheats the other, and that He leaves them once one does. A study of partnership in Islamic finance says that the narrations it cites make ethical integrity and mutual trust the very foundation of partnership in Islam.
rows.why: These texts are read as a call for caution: partners often compromise each other's rights, and partnership rests on integrity and mutual trust.

rows.scholar: Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Quduri al-Baghdadi
rows.new_version_name: Classical scheme: ownership partnership vs contract partnership, with four contract kinds (mufawadah, 'inan, crafts, wujuh)
rows.what_changed: Al-Quduri, a jurist of the Hanafi school who died in 1037 and was buried in Baghdad, set out the kinds of partnership in his law book. Partnership is of two kinds: one not based on a contract (sharikat al-milk) and one made by contract. Contract partnership, al-Quduri wrote, comes in four kinds. In the mufawadah kind the partners are equal in their wealth. The limited kind ('inan) is built on each partner acting as the other's agent, without each standing surety for the other. Two tailors or two dyers may also be partners on the basis that both accept work. In the partnership called wujuh, the partnership is valid when neither partner has property. A modern overview notes that the Hanafi school divides partnership into two categories, and that the mufawadah, with complete equality in wealth or capital, profit and work, is accepted only by the Hanafi school. By contrast, the limited partnership ('inan) is described as the most widely accepted form, recognised by all.
rows.why: Partnership can arise either from owning something jointly or from an agreement, and a jointly bought asset already makes its buyers partners in ownership. The contract kinds differ in their basis: equal wealth, agency without surety, shared work, or no property at all.
rejected_by: Shafi'i (rejects the labour partnership as invalid)

rows.scholar: Shafi'i school (as summarised by 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jaziri)
rows.new_version_name: Shafi'i restriction: only the limited partnership ('inan) is valid
rows.what_changed: In the Shafi'i school's view, only one kind of partnership is allowed: the limited partnership ('inan). A survey of the law of the four schools by 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jaziri reports that, for the Shafi'is, the other kinds named in other schools are void, and that they fall into three groups. The first is the partnership of bodies (abdan), where two or more people join and each practises a craft. Another is the partnership of reputation (wujuh), where two or more people of standing join to buy goods for trade. A modern study likewise says that, for the Shafi'i school, the labour partnership is invalid. Other schools went the other way: the Hanafi and Hanbali schools allow the labour partnership and the partnership of reputation, while the Maliki school allows a labour partnership when the partners work in the same profession. The same study says the Hanbali and Maliki schools do not require the partners in a mufawadah to be equal in every respect.
rows.why: The disputed kinds are those based on the partners' expertise in a profession or on their reputation. In the partnership of reputation the partners have no investment at all.
rejected_by: Hanbali (both permit the labour partnership and the partnership of reputation)

rows.scholar: Ottoman commission headed by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha (the Mecelle / Majalla)
rows.new_version_name: Codified partnership law: the Ottoman Mecelle (Majalla), Book X on joint ownership
rows.what_changed: In the late nineteenth century the Ottoman Empire put this law into a civil code, the Mecelle, whose substance was based on the Hanafi tradition. It was issued in sixteen volumes from 1869 to 1876 and came into force in 1877. A commission headed by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha prepared it. Its book on joint ownership divides it into joint ownership of property held in absolute ownership and joint ownership arising from a contract. It defines a contract of partnership as a contract for joint ownership in which two or more persons share in capital and profit. It recognises partnership in property, in work and on credit, and partnerships with unequal shares. A partnership for work is made to undertake work, and a partnership may also be made with no capital, in which the partners buy and sell on credit. The code remained the basis of civil law in Jordan and Kuwait.
rows.why: The code set out in articles rules based on the Hanafi legal tradition, which had official status in the Empire.

rows.year_how_known: year the doctoral thesis was submitted to Cairo University, as the pages state
rows.scholar: Sami Hassan (also written Sami Hammud)
rows.new_version_name: Diminishing partnership (musharakah mutanaqisah)
rows.what_changed: A modified form of partnership, the diminishing partnership (musharakah mutanaqisah), is commonly used. Two parties are partners in a project that earns income, and one of them undertakes to buy the other's share gradually. The idea originated in a doctoral thesis by Dr Sami Hassan, submitted to Cairo University in 1976. One of the earliest recorded uses of the model was in Egypt. In 1978 the Jordan Islamic Bank wrote the term into its legal framework, and Jordan's Islamic bank law of that year used it for financing and investment. In 1979, at the first international conference of Islamic financial institutions in Dubai, it was accepted as a workable new way to invest and finance. In one use, the bank rents its share in a property to the client, and as the client gradually buys the bank's share, the rent goes down in proportion. Because the arrangement combines several contracts, modern jurists disagree about it.
rows.why: The form lets one partner buy the other's share step by step. The client's rent to the bank falls as the client buys the bank's share in the property.

rows.scholar: Muhammad Taqi Usmani
rows.new_version_name: Musharakah as a bank financing mode (single deal, running account, house finance)
rows.what_changed: Writing in 1998, Muhammad Taqi Usmani noted that the word musharakah itself is not found in the books of Islamic law (fiqh). He explained that writers on Islamic ways of financing brought the term in recently, and that it normally means one kind of partnership: the partnership in capital, where two or more people invest in a joint business. He called musharakah and mudarabah the real and ideal tools of financing in Islamic law. He showed how they can finance a single transaction, and how institutions fund a running business by opening a running account for it. Profit on such an account is worked out on a daily product basis at the end of the term. For house finance, he described the financier's share being divided into equal units, which the client promises to buy one at a time, with the rent falling each time.
rows.why: Usmani held that musharakah can play a vital role in an economy built on Islamic principles, and saw partnership as the ideal way to finance.

rows.scholar: International Islamic Fiqh Academy (Resolution No. 136 (2/15))
rows.new_version_name: Diminishing partnership approved with conditions (fiqh academy ruling)
rows.what_changed: The International Islamic Fiqh Academy at first put off a decision on the diminishing partnership, at a session in Kuwait City, so that it could be studied further. At its fifteenth session, held in Muscat in March 2004, it ruled the form permissible as long as it follows the general rules of partnership. It described it as a partnership in a project that earns income, in which one party undertakes to buy the other's share gradually. Only one of the parties may give a binding undertaking to buy out the other. The shares must be bought at their market value. Each party bears any loss in line with its share of the capital. One partner may rent the other partner's share for a specific amount. The profits of each party must be set in the contract as percentage shares.
rows.why: The academy tied its approval to the general rules of partnership, and set out that each party bears loss by its share of capital and that shares are bought at market value.

rows.new_version_name: Partnership certificates (sukuk al-musharakah) with purchase undertaking
rows.what_changed: The partnership became a structure used in a significant number of large sukuk issues, the musharakah sukuk. The issuer raises cash by selling sukuk and puts that cash into the partnership. Examples named in one paper are a 3.5 billion US dollar issue by PCFC Development FZCO (DP World) in 2006 and a 7.5 billion dirham issue by JAFZ Sukuk Limited in 2007. The purchase price promised in such deals was normally the original book value, which matched the face amount of the sukuk. Muhammad Taqi Usmani objected that this promise breaks the duty to share risk in musharakah and mudarabah sukuk. He was reported as saying that about 85 per cent of sukuk did not comply with Islamic law because of repurchase agreements. He said fixed income might be possible in leasing (ijarah) sukuk, but not in partnership sukuk. The report adds that the certificates should be bought at market value at maturity, which would in effect make them an equity instrument.
rows.why: Partnership certificates let an issuer raise cash for the partnership by issuing sukuk, while the promised buy-back price matched the sukuk's face or principal amount.

rows.scholar: Qur'an (al-Muzzammil 73:20, the phrase darb fi'l-ard)
rows.new_version_name: Root: 'travelling in the land' to seek God's bounty (darb fi'l-ard)
rows.what_changed: The Qur'an never names this contract. Its usual name, mudarabah, comes from the phrase al-darb fi al-ard, which does appear in the Qur'an, but the term itself has no explicit basis in the Qur'an or in the Prophet's practice. Among its meanings is moving from place to place in search of a living. Modern writers link it to the verse of Surah al-Muzzammil (73:20) about others who travel the land seeking God's bounty. Muslim scholars agree that the name is rooted in this phrase. The Hanafi jurist al-Sarakhsi explained the word as coming from the idea of making a journey. Another name for it, qirad, is said literally to mean cutting money and distance. Many Islamic traditions instead attribute the contract's origin to the Prophet and his companions.
rows.why: The contract took this name because it involves travelling to trade. The Qur'an supplies only the phrase the name comes from; the term itself has no explicit basis there.

rows.scholar: Arabian caravan trade practice; the Prophet Muhammad as working partner for Khadija bint Khuwaylid
rows.new_version_name: Caravan profit-sharing: the Prophet trades with Khadija's capital
rows.what_changed: Before Islam, this kind of profit-sharing was already a common way of doing business in Arabia. Arabs, especially the Quraysh tribe, travelled with caravans to trade. The arrangement was one of the most practical ways to meet the short-term funding needs of caravan trade. Before his prophethood, Muhammad travelled to Syria on business. On these trading trips Khadija supplied the capital and Muhammad supplied the work, acting as her agent. According to one study, she promised to give him twice as much of the profits as other merchants. Jurists rely on this deal, which one account places about a year and two months before the two married. One study holds that the technique was tacitly approved (taqrir) by him, by way of relaxation (rukhsa).
rows.why: Caravan trade needed short-term funding, and pairing an owner of money with a travelling trader met that need.

rows.scholar: Companions of the Prophet (the caliphs Umar ibn al-Khattab and Uthman ibn Affan)
rows.new_version_name: Qirad of the Companions, accepted by consensus
rows.what_changed: The Hanafi jurist al-Kasani reports that the Companions practised this contract and that the Prophet never voiced disapproval of it. In one recorded case, two sons of Umar ibn al-Khattab, on the way home from an army in Iraq, passed by Abu Musa al-Ashari, the governor of Basra. The account mentions some of God's property that was to be sent to the Commander of the Faithful. A man sitting with Umar suggested making it a qirad. Umar agreed, and he took the principal and half of the profit. Another report says Uthman ibn Affan gave money as qirad on condition that the profit be shared. Later writers state that the Companions agreed it was permitted. One study adds that, unlike musaqat and muzara'a, its validity enjoys consensus in most of its conditions. Scholars still counted it as an exception, because it hires a worker for a wage that is not known in advance.
rows.why: People with spare money often could not invest it themselves, so the law allowed this exception out of necessity.

rows.new_version_name: Qirad in its Hijazi (Maliki) form: the first written rulebook in al-Muwatta
rows.what_changed: Malik ibn Anas, who lived from 711 to 795, compiled al-Muwatta, one of the earliest collections of hadith texts. One version of the book became the standard text of the Maliki school. Its book on qirad records the cases of Umar and Uthman. The book says qirad is only good with gold or silver coin and never with goods. The investor may not tie the worker to buying from one named person. The worker does not guarantee the capital, and when travelling he pays for his food and clothing out of it. The name qirad was the one favoured in the Hijaz, while people in Iraq preferred mudaraba. Later the Maliki and Shafi'i schools kept the term qirad, while the Hanafis and Hanbalis used mudarabah. The words differ, but they carry no real difference in meaning.
rows.why: Under these rules the worker does not guarantee the capital. The different names most likely began as a matter of region.

rows.scholar: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani (later Hanafi jurists al-Sarakhsi and al-Kasani)
rows.new_version_name: Mudarabah in its Iraqi (Hanafi) form: unrestricted and restricted mandates
rows.what_changed: The name mudaraba, a synonym of qirad, was preferred by the Iraqis, and the Hanafi and Hanbali schools adopted that term. Al-Shaybani, who died in 805, played a key part in organising and passing on Hanafi law. His Kitab al-Asl contains a book on mudaraba, the Kitab al-Mudarabah. Hanafi jurists gave the working partner a scope for independent action that differs from the other schools. In the unlimited form, the investor lets the worker act fully at his own discretion in all business matters. In a limited mandate, the worker's freedom is set by the terms the investor lays down. Modern writers call these two forms unrestricted mudarabah, where the manager may invest in any business he thinks fit, and restricted mudarabah, where the capital provider names a particular business or sets conditions. The worker could also invest the capital in a second mudarabah, known as al-mudarib yudarib.
rows.why: The two forms differ in how much freedom the investor gives the worker: full discretion, or only what the investor's terms allow.

rows.what_changed: In 1966 al-Arabi also proposed a banking system with mudarabah at its centre. He went further with a two-tier mudarabah, in which the bank collects savings on a mudarabah basis and places the funds on a mudarabah basis too. Toward its depositors, the bank would act as the mudarib. In 1968 Siddiqi wrote a pioneering and fairly detailed outline of Islamic banking in Urdu. Siddiqi proposed a two-tier model with mudarabah as the main mode, backed by fixed-return tools such as mark-up sale and leasing. In this design, instead of the bank and its depositors owning the capital and the entrepreneur acting as mudarib, the bank and the entrepreneur are both mudarib, and losses left after overhead and operating expenses pass to the depositors. One writer notes that because the entrepreneur could invest the capital of a first mudaraba in a second one, known as al-mudarib yudarib, the structure allows financial intermediation like that of modern banks.
rows.why: A second tier is used when the bank lacks the capacity to be the investor or the skill to be the fund manager. It let one contract cover both sides of a bank, deposits and financing.

rows.what_changed: One study names as the highest-profile experiment the Mit Ghamr local savings bank, set up in Egypt by Ahmed El-Najjar in 1963. It neither charged nor paid interest and shared in the profits of small businesses. Its depositors were paid less when those ventures earned less than expected. When commercial Islamic banks first appeared in the mid-1970s, they used mudaraba as the model for their operations. Dubai Islamic Bank was set up in 1975, though one study stresses that the industry did not begin there. Islamic banks tried to apply mudarabah through a product called the investment account. Under the historical doctrines of Islamic law, the bank, as entrepreneur, cannot guarantee the depositors' capital. One study finds the product tends to be a poorer substitute for a guaranteed, fixed-rate deposit, and that none has matched the true spirit of profit-and-loss sharing. Another study notes that mudarabah and musharakah, which early banking theory took as the foundation of Islamic banking, are used far less than other forms of Islamic financing such as murabahah.

rows.what_changed: At its fourth session in Jeddah in February 1988, the Islamic Fiqh Academy ruled on muqaradah certificates. It described them as investment tools that split qirad capital into certificates of equal value, registered to their owners as joint owners of the venture. It preferred to call them muqaradah bonds. The person who receives the money to invest in the project is the mudarib. Neither the prospectus nor the bonds may carry a guarantee from the fund manager of the capital or of a fixed profit. If such a guarantee is made, the condition is void, and the mudarib is entitled to the profit of a similar mudarabah. The prospectus or certificates may include a promise by a third party to donate a specific amount, with no return, to meet losses in a project, provided that commitment is independent of the mudarabah contract. The certificates may be traded on stock markets. The resolution refers to the conclusions of a seminar the Academy organised with the Islamic Research and Training Institute of the Islamic Development Bank on 2–5 September 1987. One reference work says the Fiqh Academy of the OIC legitimised the use of sukuk in February 1988.
rows.why: The Academy saw this form as useful for developing public resources by bringing money and work together.

rows.new_version_name: Bay' / tijarah (sale and trade), Qur'an 2:275 and 4:29: the general permission of sale
rows.what_changed: The word murabaha itself does not appear in the Qur'an or in the hadith, although a verb derived from the word ribh appears in one verse (2:16). Instead, a sale at cost plus a fixed profit is counted under the general Qur'anic ruling on sale in verses 2:275 and 4:29, and for that reason there is no disagreement about whether it is allowed. A modern fatwa page cites verse 2:275, which says that God has permitted trade. The same page notes that no hadith is known that singles out murabaha from other kinds of sale. It quotes Ibn Qudamah as saying the sale is permissible and that there is no difference of opinion about its validity. It also cites the general rule that the basic principle in transactions is that they are permitted. It defines the contract simply as the sale of goods at cost plus a known profit mark-up.
rows.why: Because no verse or hadith names murabaha, its legal footing is the Qur'an's general permission of sale and trade rather than a text of its own.

rows.year_how_known: death year of Ali ibn Abi Talib, given on the page as 40 AH (about 661 CE); the page calls his saying the first recorded use of the word tawarruq
rows.scholar: Ali ibn Abi Talib (first recorded use of the word); later Hanafi and Hanbali jurists
rows.new_version_name: Tawarruq (buying on credit to resell for cash): the classical, individual form
rows.what_changed: In legal usage, tawarruq means that a person buys a commodity on credit and sells it to someone other than the original seller for cash, in most cases at a price lower than the purchase price. One study traces the first recorded use of the word to Ali ibn Abi Talib, who died in the year 40 of the Islamic calendar. The classical form is simple and individual, with nothing arranged in advance. It differs from the buy-back sale called inah, in which both sales take place between the same seller and buyer with no third party. For most Hanafi scholars the two-party inah is disliked, but individual tawarruq, where the buyer sells the goods to a third party, is permitted. Ibn al-Qayyim reported that his teacher Ibn Taymiyyah prohibited tawarruq and kept prohibiting it even when people asked him again and again to allow it. One view in the debate held that tawarruq is worse than riba because it brings a higher cost and losses. Even so, the dominant view of the later Hanbali scholars moved towards allowing it. Much later, in April 2009, the International Islamic Fiqh Academy ruled that this form, buying on credit and selling to someone other than the original seller, is permitted as long as it meets the conditions of sale that Shariah accepts.
rows.why: Tawarruq turns a purchase on credit into cash, through a resale for cash to someone other than the original seller. For most Hanafi scholars, the resale to a third party is what set permitted tawarruq apart from the disliked two-party inah, in which both sales are between the same seller and buyer.

rows.scholar: Malik ibn Anas (al-Muwatta)
rows.new_version_name: Murabaha by name: resale on a stated cost, with rules on which costs may be added
rows.what_changed: Malik ibn Anas, who lived from about 711 to 795 and gave his name to the Maliki school of Sunni law, discussed murabaha by name in his book al-Muwatta. His example is a man who buys cloth in one city and takes it to another city to sell it as a murabaha. He rules that the cost of carrying the cloth is included in the basic price. Work done on the goods, such as bleaching, tailoring and dyeing, is treated in the same way as the cloth itself. But the seller may not count the wage of an agent or allowances for ironing, folding and similar expenses. Malik also takes up the case of a seller who says the goods cost him a set sum, such as one hundred dinars. A modern study likewise discusses what follows if any misrepresentation is discovered in a murabaha sale. A modern Islamic encyclopedia notes that the Malikis did not regard such sales as preferable, because of the problems that can arise when the cost is not stated truthfully.
rows.why: Malik's example of cloth carried from one city to another for resale as murabaha called for rules on which expenses could be added to the stated cost and which could not.

rows.scholar: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (Kitab al-Umm)
rows.new_version_name: The purchase-order sale with a non-binding promise (al-Shafi'i, al-Umm)
rows.what_changed: Al-Shafi'i, who lived from 767 to 820 and founded the Shafi'i school of Sunni law, described in al-Umm a case in which one person shows another a commodity and asks him to buy it for him in return for a set profit. A Jordanian fatwa page says scholars call this arrangement murabaha for the purchase orderer. That page requires the financing party to take actual possession of the commodity before selling it to the buyer. It also requires that the buyer not be forced to take the commodity if he decides to back out. A study of the modern debate notes that al-Shafi'i clearly states that if the arrangement is treated as binding, the transaction becomes invalid. Another study of early opinions finds that most early scholars prohibited this kind of transaction when it included a negotiation or a promise of profit. Sami Hasan Hammoud, who first introduced this concept to Islamic banking in his PhD thesis, based his model mainly on examples given by al-Shafi'i.
rows.why: In the arrangement one person asks another to buy a commodity for him for a set profit, and the buyer may still go on with the deal or back out of it. In al-Shafi'i's view, treating the arrangement as binding would make the transaction invalid.

rows.scholar: Classical jurists of the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools (al-Marghinani and Ibn Jazzi named on the pages)
rows.new_version_name: The trust-sale family: murabaha, tawliyah and wadi'ah, set against the bargained sale (musawamah)
rows.what_changed: The classical jurists sorted sales by the way the price is set: either trust (amana) is the key element, or bargaining (musawamah) is. In a bargained sale, as the Maliki jurist Ibn Jazzi defined it, the buyer negotiates with the seller over a price until they agree. Sales of trust were of three kinds: murabaha, tawliyah and wadi'ah. In murabaha the goods are resold with a stated surcharge that represents the profit. In tawliyah the price equals the value of the goods as the seller states it, with no profit or loss. In wadi'ah the price is set below what the seller says the goods are worth. The schools phrased the definition of murabaha in different words. The Shafi'i and Hanbali schools define it as selling at the original price plus, say, one dirham of profit for every ten, on condition that both sides know the original price. Another definition describes the seller selling for the price he paid, with a profit known to both seller and buyer. A Hanafi definition speaks of transferring ownership of a commodity in exchange for the original price with a profit added. Al-Marghinani, who died in 593 AH, held in al-Hidayah that the sale is lawful because it meets all the conditions for validity.
rows.why: These were called sales of trust because the seller is to be taken at his word, and the plain meaning of trust (amana) is the opposite of betrayal.

rows.year_how_known: Year of Hammoud's PhD thesis, cited as 1976, and of his recommendation of murabaha to the Islamic Development Bank and Dubai Islamic Bank, as the pages state
rows.scholar: Sami Hasan Hamoud
rows.new_version_name: Murabaha to the purchase orderer: the bank's three-party murabaha
rows.what_changed: In 1976 Sami Hasan Hamoud, an Islamic banker, introduced this arrangement to Islamic banking in his PhD thesis. He based his model mainly on examples given by al-Shafi'i. In the modern form the customer asks the bank to buy goods, the bank buys them from a third party, and the customer promises to buy them from the bank once it owns them. The bank then adds a mark-up to its cost and sells the goods to the customer on credit. In the same year Hamoud recommended murabaha to the Islamic Development Bank and to Dubai Islamic Bank. A thesis on project finance, discussing mark-up financing, noted that this form of financing was being widely used by the Islamic Development Bank. An encyclopedia entry credits Hamoud with developing the concept and says it became popular shortly after. Most current Islamic banking practice rests on the premise that promises are binding. Estimates of its weight vary: one puts it at 80% of Islamic lending, another at almost 90% or more of Islamic banking finance. Critics see this large-scale use of murabaha as a departure from Islamic banking principles. They also complain that in most real transactions the goods never change hands.
rows.why: Modern murabaha rests on a bank buying goods and reselling them, at a mark-up and on credit, to the customers who asked for them, in a model Hamoud based mainly on examples from al-Shafi'i.

rows.scholar: International Islamic Fiqh Academy (Organization of the Islamic Conference)
rows.new_version_name: Murabaha to the purchase orderer with an enforceable promise (Fiqh Academy Resolutions 40–41)
rows.what_changed: In December 1988, at its fifth session in Kuwait City, the International Islamic Fiqh Academy ruled on murabaha to the purchase orderer and on keeping promises. It allowed the sale on goods already in the seller's physical possession, provided the seller carries the risk of loss before delivery. It said a promise is morally binding on the person who makes it, unless he has a valid excuse. It added that a promise is legally binding when it is made conditional on an obligation, and that it must then be fulfilled or damages paid. A mutual promise between the two parties is allowed in a murabaha sale only if one or both of them keep an option. A study of the debate says the OIC's Islamic Fiqh Academy regards one-sided promises in commercial dealings as binding if the promisor caused the other side to take on liabilities or expenses. The same study notes that Muslim scholars agree promises are ethically binding, but only the Maliki school holds that they are also legally binding. The Academy also asked Islamic banks to study the practical side of this sale.
rows.why: The ruling made a promise legally binding when it is made conditional on an obligation, while the seller still carries the risk of loss before delivery.

rows.scholar: Malaysian Islamic banking practice
rows.new_version_name: Bay' bithaman ajil (BBA): the long-term deferred-payment sale of Malaysian banks
rows.what_changed: Islamic banking in Malaysia dates from the 1980s. Short-term repayment is known as murabahah, while long-term repayment is called BBA, meaning deferred payment. The buyer must repay the whole mark-up price to the Islamic bank in instalments, and the selling price includes the cost plus a profit margin. One source distinguishes murabahah from BBA products: in BBA, disclosure of the cost price of the item being financed is not a condition of the contract. One study states that BBA involves no transfer of ownership, only a right to a registrable interest. The courts are divided into two on the bank's right to impose the entire sale price. One study states that the profit margin still charged for the unexpired part of the term cannot be actual profit. Another study states that it is unfair for the bank to collect the entire sale price when the facility has been ended early. One writer quoted in a study said he would prefer that deferred sale (bai' al-muajjal) be removed from the list of permissible methods altogether.
rows.why: Short-term repayment was known as murabahah and long-term repayment as BBA, under which the buyer repays the whole mark-up price to the bank in instalments.

rows.year_how_known: year of the ruling: Resolution 179 (5/19), 19th session of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy, Sharjah, 26–30 April 2009
rows.scholar: Islamic banks' treasury practice; ruled on by the International Islamic Fiqh Academy
rows.new_version_name: Commodity murabaha and organized (structured) tawarruq
rows.what_changed: Commodity murabaha is a variant of murabaha to the purchase orderer in which an Islamic bank first buys an asset from a commodity broker and then sells it to the customer. It was introduced in the Malaysian market as a treasury product, and Islamic banks also use it with conventional banks for interbank liquidity. The underlying asset is usually a base metal. One study notes that commodity murabaha and organized tawarruq follow the same procedure and mechanism. One study says that taking real delivery is technically impossible because the commodities do not move from the warehouses. In April 2009, at its 19th session in Sharjah, the International Islamic Fiqh Academy ruled on the types of tawarruq. It described structured tawarruq as a case where a person buys goods on credit and the financier arranges their resale, directly, through an agent or in collusion with the buyer. Inverse tawarruq takes the same form, except that the institution is the mustawriq and the client is the financier. The Academy prohibited both forms because they involve explicit, implicit or customary collusion that works as a trick to get cash now for a larger future debt, which is riba. The Board of Iftaa', Research and Islamic Studies also declared organized tawarruq by some Islamic banks forbidden, citing the Academy's 2009 resolution. Bankers welcomed the resolution in principle, but a number of them wanted further clarification.
rows.why: Islamic banks deal with conventional banks through commodity murabaha for interbank liquidity. The Academy prohibited these forms because their collusion makes a trick for getting cash now for a larger future debt, which is riba.

rows.new_version_name: Classical ijarah: sale of known benefits (usufruct) of things or of people's services
rows.what_changed: All the schools of law agree that ijarah is a contract selling known and specified benefits or services in return for compensation. A modern study sums this up by calling ijarah a sale of benefits, or usufruct, usually of goods that last. It covers the sale of the use of both physical things and living beings. Among hired workers, one who works for an individual is set apart from one who serves the general public, such as tailors. For the Hanafis, a benefit is not property, so it cannot be inherited, and the lease ends when one of the two parties dies. The Maliki and Hanbali definitions add that the benefit must be a lawful one. Ibn Qudamah, a Hanbali jurist who died in Damascus in 1223 and whose best-known book is al-Mughni, reported that scholars of all regions and all times agree that leasing is lawful. A dissenting view came from Abdurrahman Ibn al-Asamm, who called leasing unlawful because it is an aleatory, or chance-based, contract, but the fatwa that reports this calls the correct view that leasing is lawful.
rows.why: All the schools treat payment for known and specified benefits or services, whether of things or of living beings, as a sale in return for compensation.
rejected_by: Abdurrahman Ibn al-Asamm (individual scholar; the page names no school)

rows.scholar: Classical Sunni jurists (earliest dated text cited: Ibn Juzay al-Kalbi, al-Qawanin al-Fiqhiyyah)
rows.new_version_name: Ijarah mawsufah fi al-dhimmah (forward lease of a described benefit)
rows.what_changed: A further kind of lease has as its subject a benefit to be delivered in the future: the benefit is well defined, but the particular unit that will provide it is not identified. Its subject matter may be non-existent or not owned. Apart from that, it follows the same rules as an ordinary lease. In his book al-Qawanin al-Fiqhiyyah, the jurist Ibn Juzay al-Kalbi gave the case of a hired animal: if the animal was owed as a described obligation and not singled out, the lessor must replace it with another animal. It is similar to salam, the sale paid in advance, because in both the thing owed is a described obligation. Some modern writers, among them Nazih Hammad and Ahmad Nassar, read the Hanafi school as forbidding it, because the leased item must be singled out for a lease to be valid. A survey of the schools replied that the classical texts of most schools discuss this contract in the same way, and that the classical scholars of the four Sunni schools agreed it is lawful. Islamic banks now use it both on its own and as part of other contracts, since it helps meet the financial needs of those who cannot afford to buy the goods or services they need in cash.
rows.why: It lets a lease cover a benefit to be delivered in the future, and it is similar to salam because in both the thing owed is a described obligation. Today it helps meet the financial needs of those who cannot afford to buy the goods or services they need in cash.
rejected_by: Hanafi school (as some modern writers read it; the survey disputes this reading)

rows.scholar: Bank Islam Malaysia Berhad (bank practice)
rows.new_version_name: Islamic hire-purchase: al-ijarah thumma al-bay' (AITAB), lease then sale
rows.what_changed: Islamic hire-purchase is one of the latest innovative products of Islamic banks, and this transaction is not recognised in classical jurisprudence. Contemporary scholars put its structure together by combining a lease contract with a sale contract. Under the first contract the customer hires the goods from the owner for an agreed rent over a set period, and under a second contract the customer buys the goods from the owner at an agreed price. In Malaysia this is called al-ijarah thumma al-bay', or AITAB. Bank Islam Malaysia, set up in 1983, was the first bank to offer it, and conventional banks later took it up too. A Malaysian study says Bank Islam brought it in from its founding under the name ijarah muntahiya bi al-tamlik. Since it began, AITAB has been governed by the Hire-Purchase Act 1967. Bank Muamalat Malaysia began offering this financing in 2000. One study notes two concerns about it: the purchase price of the leased asset is not a real price, and the deal appears similar to a conditional sale. One study notes that the lease and the sale are put in one trading document.
rows.why: It was designed to meet current demand and avoid certain risks in financing household goods and motor vehicles.

rows.what_changed: Islamic financial institutions use leasing as a way of financing, so that customers can use durable goods and equipment such as ships, aircraft and heavy machines. At its third session, held in Amman in October 1986, the Fiqh Academy answered questions from the Islamic Development Bank about its leasing. The bank would buy equipment for a client, intending to lease it to that client once the client had received it. The Academy accepted as lawful the bank's promise to lease the equipment to the client after the bank had become its owner. The lease agreement was to be carried out after the equipment had actually been acquired and taken into possession. As owner, the bank carried the risk of loss and of manufacturing defects. The Academy also allowed the bank to promise to give the equipment away to the client at the end of the lease period.

rows.new_version_name: Caution on rent-to-own: a plain lease with options at the end preferred
rows.what_changed: At its fifth session, held in Kuwait City in December 1988, the Fiqh Academy looked at rent-to-own contracts. It said that it is a priority to avoid rent-to-own forms and to use other options instead. One option it named was a rental contract in which the lessor gives the lessee a choice once all the instalments have been paid. The lessee could end the rental and return the property to its owner. Or the lessee could buy the rented item at its market value when the rental ends. It said there are many other forms of rent-to-own contracts, and it put off debate on them to its next session, until it received sample contracts.
rows.why: The Academy gave priority to avoiding rent-to-own forms and preferred other options, while it waited for sample contracts before judging the remaining forms.

rows.year_how_known: year of the ruling: the resolution page gives the 12th session in Riyadh, 23-28 September 2000
rows.scholar: International Islamic Fiqh Academy (OIC)
rows.new_version_name: Ijarah muntahia bittamleek (lease ending in ownership) with separate contracts
rows.what_changed: The lease that ends with the lessee owning the asset, called ijarah wa iqtina' and also al-ijarah muntahia bittamleek, is widely practised because it is akin to murabahah, the cost-plus sale. At its twelfth session in Riyadh, in September 2000, the Fiqh Academy set out which versions of it are lawful. It banned any version that joins two different contracts over the same item, at the same time and for the same period. So ownership may not pass to the lessee in return for the rent paid, with the lease simply turning into a sale on its own. It allowed a lease paired with a separate gift contract that takes effect at the end of the lease once all rent is paid, or a lease that gives the lessee an option to buy the property. The two contracts must be fully separate in time, and both parties must genuinely want to conclude the lease and not use it as a mere cover for the sale. The owner, not the lessee, must bear the risk to the asset and pay for its upkeep, apart from running costs. The Academy put off its ruling on leasing bonds.
rows.why: The Academy prohibited joining two different contracts over the same item at the same time, and required both parties to genuinely want the lease and not use it as a cover for the sale.

rows.new_version_name: Sukuk al-ijarah (lease-based investment certificates)
rows.what_changed: Such trust instruments were named in Arabic sukuk or sukuk al-ijarah. In 2001 the State of Bahrain offered its first sukuk al-ijarah in its home market, worth 250 million US dollars over five years. The underlying assets were bought from the seller and at once leased to the lessee; the lease creates rental income for a special purpose company, which issues sukuk meant to represent undivided shared ownership. The user also promises to buy the assets when the lease ends. Malaysia's 600-million-dollar global sukuk of June 2002 was the first sukuk listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange, and Qatar followed with a 700-million-dollar issue in 2003. At its session in Muscat in March 2004, the Fiqh Academy described these certificates as equal shares in the ownership of assets or benefits that earn income. It allowed holders to sell them on a secondary market, as long as each certificate stands for ownership of real assets leased out for income. Such a security must reflect the holder's share in an underlying asset or enterprise, and the legal nature of a conventional bond is clearly against Islamic law.
rows.why: The legal nature of a conventional bond is clearly against Islamic law, and an Islamic security must reflect the holder's share in an underlying asset or enterprise. Certificates that stand for ownership of tangible assets leased out for income may be sold on a secondary market to any buyer.

rows.new_version_name: Maliki salam: set description, no unripe crops, short delay of capital allowed
rows.what_changed: Malik reports that Abdullah ibn Umar said there was no harm in paying a man in advance for food, provided the food had a set description. The price and the delivery date must also be fixed, and the advance may not be made for crops or dates that have not begun to ripen. Malik also set out the practice for someone who makes an advance for foodstuffs, saying that in the case he describes the buyer must take back only exactly the silver, gold or price he paid. A later reference work reports that the Maliki school allows the buyer to delay handing over the salam capital for two or three days. The same work states that it is a condition that the capital be delivered at the meeting where the contract is made. A modern study gives the Maliki limit as no more than three days, whether or not this was agreed in advance. Malik, who died in 795, is the scholar after whom the Maliki school is named.
rows.why: The conditions reported from Ibn Umar tie the advance to food with a set description, price and date, and keep it away from crops that have not begun to ripen.

rows.new_version_name: Hanafi salam: goods present throughout the term, no animals
rows.what_changed: The Hanafi jurist al-Quduri, author of the Mukhtasar, died in 1037. He allowed salam in anything that can be described, or whose measure can be known, accurately. But he required the goods paid for to be present from the moment of the contract until the delivery date. He also ruled out salam in animals and in their parts, such as feet, skins and bones. The seller must take the price before the two parties separate, or the salam is not valid. A modern study notes that on animals the Maliki, Shafi'i and the reliable Hanbali position allow salam, while the Hanafi school does not. The same study records the Hanafi view that the goods must be available from the conclusion of the contract until maturity.
rows.why: The Hanafi rule limited salam to goods that can be described accurately and that are present from the contract until delivery.

rows.new_version_name: Salam as articles of a written civil code
rows.what_changed: The Mejelle, composed between 1869 and 1876, was an attempt to write Hanafi law on civil dealings into a code. One of its articles defines salam as a sale by immediate payment against future delivery. Another states that salam is concluded, like an ordinary sale, by offer and acceptance. For salam to stay valid, the price must be settled in the meeting where the contract is concluded; if the parties part before then, the contract is revoked. A modern study notes that the Mejelle has no article on whether salam in animals is lawful.
rows.why: The code was built on the Hanafi school and was an attempt to codify its rules on civil dealings.

rows.scholar: Islamic banks (bank practice)
rows.new_version_name: Parallel salam (back-to-back salam) in Islamic banking
rows.what_changed: Today, salam is widely practised by Islamic banks. A bank may sell such goods on through a parallel salam with the same delivery date. One rulebook calls this a back-to-back contract, in which the bank sells goods of the same specification as those bought under salam to someone other than the original seller. This lets the bank fix a price now for future delivery, hedging its price risk, and spares it from taking delivery of the goods and storing them. The rulebook stresses that the bank's duties under the two contracts are not conditional on, or dependent on, each other. So there is no legal basis for setting off the bank's credit exposure under one contract against the other. A modern study notes that Sudan, as a farming country, has a large demand for salam-based arrangements.
rows.why: The second contract protects the bank against price changes and saves it from having to take in and store the goods itself.

rows.scholar: Abu Hanifa and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan
rows.new_version_name: Hanafi istisna by juristic preference (istihsan), not binding before acceptance
rows.what_changed: The Hanafi school declared istisna valid on the basis of juristic preference (istihsan), the use of discretion in a legal decision. In other words, Hanafi jurists allowed it as an exception to a general rule that would otherwise forbid it. They grounded the exception in people's needs. They also pointed to practical consensus, common benefit and custom. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, a companion of Abu Hanifa, is quoted as saying that istisna is allowed by the consensus of Muslims. Even so, most Hanafi scholars saw it as a contract that, in general, does not bind the parties. According to Abu Hanifa and Muhammad, the person who placed the order could refuse the finished work if he did not like it when he saw it. Not every Hanafi agreed: Zufar kept to strict analogy and did not allow the contract.
rows.why: A general rule stood against allowing the contract, but people needed to order made goods, so the Hanafis made an exception by juristic preference. They also leaned on custom and practical consensus.

rows.what_changed: Abu Yusuf broke with the majority of Hanafi scholars, who held that istisna does not bind in general, and said that it is a binding contract in general. One study reports that he changed his earlier opinion and treated the contract as binding from its first stage. On time limits, Abu Hanifa held that the contract should be free of any specified duration, and one study states that naming a delivery period turns istisna into salam. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, by contrast, ruled that istisna is valid whether or not a delivery period is set.
rows.why: Under Abu Yusuf's view the deal was binding from its first stage. One study notes that the Mejelle also adopts Abu Yusuf's view in its article on the contract.

rows.new_version_name: Classical Hanafi formulation: istihsan plus salam-and-hire mix (al-Kasani)
rows.what_changed: Al-Kasani was a twelfth-century Sunni jurist who became an influential figure of the Hanafi school; he died in 1191, and his major work is Bada'i al-Sana'i. He admitted that by strict analogy the contract would not be allowed. He allowed it by juristic preference, because people agree on needing it and scholars agree on its use. He added that it joins two permitted contracts: salam and hire (ijarah). The maker supplies both the material and the work; if he does not, the deal becomes a hire contract. The contract is also held valid because the law sometimes treats a thing that does not yet exist as if it existed. The item must be one that people commonly order this way, so fruits and grains are left out.
rows.why: The contract failed strict analogy, so al-Kasani rested it on juristic preference and on people's agreed need and practice.

rows.year_how_known: the code was composed between 1869 and 1876 (year it was completed)
rows.scholar: Ottoman Mejelle commission headed by Ahmad Djevdet Pasha
rows.new_version_name: Codified binding istisna (Ottoman Mejelle, Article 392)
rows.what_changed: The Mejelle, a code of Islamic civil transactions prepared under the Ottoman Caliphate, was written between 1869 and 1876 as part of a law-making process. A commission of jurists led by Ahmad Djevdet Pasha drafted it. The code defines istisna as making an agreement with a craftsman to make something. It describes the case where a person asks a craftsman to make a thing for a stated sum of money and the craftsman accepts. Its Article 392 then says that once the contract is concluded, neither party may revoke it. On this point the code follows the view of Abu Yusuf, not that of most Hanafi scholars, who held the contract to be non-binding in general. A fatwa gives the same rule: once the istisna contract is concluded, neither side has the right to back out.
rows.why: The Mejelle was prepared under the Ottoman Caliphate as a code of Islamic civil transactions, as part of a law-making process. For istisna it chose Abu Yusuf's binding view, so that a concluded order could not be revoked.

rows.new_version_name: Modern binding istisna with deferred or instalment price and penalty clause (Fiqh Academy ruling)
rows.what_changed: In May 1992, the Council of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy held its seventh session in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. It ruled that the contract, which covers both work and goods, is binding on both parties once its basic conditions are met. This differs from the view of most Hanafi scholars, who had held that the contract does not bind in general. The resolution requires a clear statement of the nature, type, amount and specifications of the thing to be made. It allows the buyer to put off the whole payment or pay it in instalments. By contrast, the majority view holds istisna valid if it is based on salam, a contract whose important condition is that the full price be handed over at the meeting where the deal is made. The parties may also agree a penalty clause, except where events beyond their control (force majeure) intervene.
rows.why: The Academy said istisna plays an important role in stimulating industry and opens broad opportunities for financing.

rows.new_version_name: Parallel istisna (back-to-back bank financing)
rows.what_changed: As a modern type of istisna, an interest-free financing method called parallel istisna has been developed. In the first contract the bank acts as seller or maker toward a customer. In the second contract the bank acts as buyer and asks another company or producer to make the goods. The two contracts are independent of each other. One study calls this method the most suited to the practice of Islamic banks today, and notes that some of them are not allowed to deal directly in commerce. Istisna is now widely used by Islamic banks and financial institutions. It is used in infrastructure such as apartment buildings and to finance property still under construction, and it can also be applied in industries such as aircraft, locomotives and shipbuilding. One study objects that the bank is not really a maker, so the deal is closer to an industrial supply contract than to istisna. Another study concludes that it raises no problem in Islamic law when applied in line with its conditions.
rows.why: Some Islamic banks are not allowed to deal directly in commerce; in parallel istisna the bank sells to a customer under one contract and, as a buyer, asks another company or producer to make the same goods under a second. One study finds this method the most suited to the practice of Islamic banks today.

rows.what_changed: Istisna sukuk (certificates) are issued on an asset that will be made in the future. Such certificates have been issued to finance manufacturing and building projects. The issuer can sign a parallel istisna for a similar asset. These certificates often pair the istisna with a forward lease. One named example is the 2006 offering by the Qatar Real Estate Investment Company, which had an istisna part in its structure. The prevailing view is that these certificates cannot be traded while building is still going on. One study adds that they can change hands once the money raised has been turned into physical assets. The same study calls them a milestone in a country's economic development.
rows.why: Issuing istisna sukuk raises funds from holders, and such sukuk have been issued to finance manufacturing or building projects.

rows.scholar: Qur'an (Surah al-Kahf)
rows.new_version_name: Root: wakala, sending one person to act for others with their money (Qur'an 18:19)
rows.what_changed: In the episode of the companions in the cave, one of them is chosen and sent with the group's money to the town to bring back food. Jurists count the Qur'an, the Prophet's practice and the agreement of scholars as the proofs that the agency contract is lawful. The key word in the verse, ib'athu, is read as "send", "appoint" or "authorize". One legal work notes that the verse may be cited as evidence that agency is allowed, because sending one of them was appointing him as an agent. In legal terms, agency means authorizing another person to carry out dealings on one's behalf. The person who gives the authority is called the principal (muwakkil), and the person appointed to use it is called the agent (wakil). Muslim jurists of every school agree that agency is permissible and lawful, and no one is reported to have forbidden it.
rows.why: In the verse, one of the group is sent, or appointed, with their money, and one legal work reads that as appointing an agent.

rows.what_changed: The Prophet gave 'Urwa one dinar to buy a sheep for him. 'Urwa went beyond these instructions and made a profit, and the Prophet praised and approved what he had done. Abu Hurayra reported that the Prophet put him in charge of keeping the alms of Ramadan. The Prophet also sent assistants to collect zakat on his behalf. He told Jabir that if he met the Prophet's agent, he should take fifteen wasaq, a measure of weight, from him. Another report says he gave 'Uqba ibn 'Amir sheep to share out among the Companions. Jurists list such reports from the Sunna among the proofs that agency is lawful.

rows.what_changed: Agency is valid whether or not the agent is paid a wage. Paid agency is allowed because agency is useful work for which the agent has the right to ask for payment. When the agent is paid, the arrangement falls under the rules of hire (ijara). Unpaid agency is also allowed, and it counts as a charitable act. One study supports paid agency with a hadith of the Prophet. In that report the Prophet gave 'Uqba ibn 'Amir sheep to distribute among the Companions, and a young goat was left over after the sharing. The agent stands in a position of trust toward the principal, because he deals with goods he does not own.

rows.new_version_name: General agency versus specific agency
rows.what_changed: Agency can be divided into two types: general agency and special agency. A general agent has full permission to act in all of the principal's affairs without exception. In another kind of agency, the principal gives the agent authority to carry out a certain duty on his behalf. Agency can also be divided into absolute and restricted agency. The author of al-Hidayah states the broad rule that a person may appoint an agent for any contract he could lawfully have made himself, such as sale or marriage. The schools split over whether a general agency is valid. The Shafi'i, Hanbali, Zahiri and Zaidi schools hold that a general agency is null and void. The Hanafi and Maliki schools, together with some Imami jurists, hold that it is valid.
rows.why: The dispute is about whether one person may give an agent permission to act in all of his affairs without exception.

rows.scholar: The majority of jurists versus al-Shafi'i
rows.new_version_name: The unauthorized agent (fuduli) and later ratification
rows.what_changed: A further split concerns the acts of an unauthorized agent. Selling another person's goods or property without that person's explicit permission is called bay' al-fuduli. Muslim jurists do not agree on whether such acts are valid. The majority say the act of an unauthorized agent depends on the owner of the property ratifying it. Among Sunni jurists, the Hanafi and Maliki schools make the sale's validity depend on the owner's permission given afterwards. The main view among Shi'a jurists also treats such a sale as valid if the owner later authorizes it. Al-Shafi'i and some other jurists hold that these acts are invalid even if the owner accepts them. One account places Hanbali jurists with the Shafi'is, treating such a sale as void from the start. Some prominent Shi'a scholars, such as al-Shaykh al-Tusi, Ibn Zuhra, al-Muhaqqiq al-Ardabili and Yusuf al-Bahrani, hold it invalid even if the owner later gives permission. The case of 'Urwa, who went beyond his orders and was praised by the Prophet, is brought into this debate.
rows.why: 'Urwa, given a dinar to buy one sheep, acted on his own initiative and made a profitable deal, and the Prophet approved it.
rejected_by: Shafi'i and Hanbali (as one page reports)
some prominent Shi'a scholars (al-Tusi, Ibn Zuhra, al-Ardabili, al-Bahrani)

rows.scholar: al-Qurtubi
rows.new_version_name: Agency drawn directly from Qur'an 18:19 in legal exegesis
rows.what_changed: Al-Qurtubi was an Andalusian Sunni scholar and Maliki jurist who died in 1273. He is well known for his classical commentary on the Qur'an. Scholars drew the lawfulness of agency from many verses of the Qur'an, especially a verse of Surah al-Kahf. That verse tells the group to send one of them with their silver coin to the city, to see what food is purest there and bring back a supply. Al-Qurtubi suggests in his commentary that this verse is valid proof that agency is lawful. On this reading, appointing someone as an agent is allowed by the verse itself. The word that carries this meaning, ib'athu, is understood as "send", "appoint" or "authorize".
rows.why: The verse's word for sending can mean "appoint" or "authorize", and al-Qurtubi took the verse as valid proof that agency is lawful.

rows.scholar: Ottoman Majalla commission headed by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha
rows.new_version_name: Agency written into a state civil code (the Majalla)
rows.what_changed: The Ottoman civil code known as the Majalla was issued in volumes from 1869 to 1876 and came into force in 1877. A commission led by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha prepared it, and its content was based on the Hanafi legal tradition. Its book on agency defines agency as one person empowering another to perform some act for him. The one who gives the power is called the principal, and the one who stands in his place is called the agent. An agent's authority may be absolute, or conditional, or limited to a certain time, or subject to some other limit. If a salary for the agent was agreed when he was appointed, he is entitled to it once he has carried out the agency. Property in the agent's hands is treated as held for safe keeping, so if it is destroyed without his fault or negligence he does not have to make good the loss. The code also states that permission and ratification amount to authority to act as agent, and that later ratification has the same effect as authority given in advance.
rows.why: The Majalla was a manual for the Ottoman courts, and its content was based on the Hanafi legal tradition.

rows.scholar: Islamic financial institutions (bank practice)
rows.new_version_name: Agency as a building block inside modern Islamic bank products
rows.what_changed: Modern Islamic financial institutions use the agency contract in many of their products. In a murabaha sale, the institution appoints the customer as its agent in the first step of the deal. The customer then identifies and buys the goods on the institution's behalf. An agency agreement is not, however, a necessary condition for murabaha. Agency is also used inside partnership contracts such as mudaraba and musharaka. One kind of partnership, in which one partner buys the other partner's share gradually, is described as a bundle of contracts that includes agency, leasing and sale. In salam, the bank names someone as its agent to sell the goods in the market. In istisna', banks usually appoint the manufacturer as their agent for selling the goods. Tawarruq is usually backed by an agency contract. Other uses include letters of credit, paying and collecting bills, fund management and securitization.
rows.why: In these products, agency lets another party identify, buy or sell goods on the institution's behalf.

rows.new_version_name: Wakala model of takaful: the operator as a paid agent
rows.what_changed: Modern takaful began in Sudan in 1979 and in Malaysia in 1984. In the wakala model, the takaful operator manages the funds and charges a fixed fee called the wakala fee. The agency used in takaful is agency for a fee, called wakalah bil al-ajr. The fee can be a fixed amount or set as an agreed ratio. Bank Al-Jazira in Saudi Arabia has practised the wakala model. The model is seen as more transparent than the mudaraba model. It is also said to raise fewer Shari'ah issues and to be free from the disputed charging of expenses, including marketing commissions. Agents employed by a takaful company are also bound by an agency contract and receive their own wages and remunerations.
rows.why: Under the wakala model the operator is paid a fee for its services and does not take a share of investment profit or surplus, apart from a performance-related fee. The wakala model is considered more transparent than the mudaraba model.

rows.scholar: Sukuk market practice (issuers in the Gulf states and Malaysia)
rows.new_version_name: Investment agency (wakala bil-istithmar) in sukuk and investment accounts
rows.what_changed: In investment agency, an investor acting as principal appoints an agent to invest funds for him. The agent lends his expertise and manages the investments on the principal's behalf. In this structure the agent must be paid a fee, even a nominal one, for the agency to be valid. The investor receives only the profit return agreed at the outset. Any profit above the agreed level is kept by the agent as a performance or incentive fee. Sukuk built this way can rest on a mixed pool of assets and investments. This lets the issuer use contracts such as murabaha and istisna' that cannot be traded on the secondary market. A 2011 market report counted USD 5.3 billion of sukuk that year structured wholly or partly as wakala, up from USD 1.8 billion in the same period of the year before. The structure was considered Shari'ah-compliant in both the Gulf states and Malaysia. Wakala sukuk are described as growing in popularity because they offer considerable flexibility. A 2021 study of the Wafiyah Investment Account at Bank Islam Malaysia Berhad uses the name wakalah bi al-istithmar.
rows.why: Investment agency lets an issuer combine different assets, including contracts such as murabaha and istisna' that cannot be traded on the secondary market. The agent is paid a fee and keeps any profit above the agreed return.

rows.new_version_name: za'im - the guarantor in the Joseph story (root word)
rows.what_changed: In the story of Joseph, a herald announces that the king's measuring cup is lost and promises a camel-load of grain to whoever brings it back. He then says that he himself guarantees that reward, using the Arabic word za'im. A reading attributed to Ibn Abbas takes za'im in this verse as another word for guarantor, or kafil. A study of guarantee in Islamic law quotes this verse, rendering it as a reward of a camel load for whoever brings the king's beaker. The other common word for guarantor, kafil, appears in a different verse, where people who swear oaths are said to have made God their guarantor. The word kafala itself comes from a verb meaning to guarantee, warrant, secure or sponsor. A modern study states that the contract is allowed on the basis of the Qur'an, the Prophet's practice and the agreement of jurists.
rows.why: The verse shows a promise of reward that the herald himself stands behind and guarantees.

rows.what_changed: Al-Bukhari's chapter on kafala describes a pledge given to a creditor that the debtor will be present at a set place to pay a debt or fine, or to face punishment. In one report there, a zakat collector sent by Umar took personal sureties for an accused man until they reached Umar. The same chapter tells of people who were told to repent and give personal sureties, and who repented while their relatives stood as sureties for them. The Hanafi jurist al-Quduri states that guarantee of the person is allowed, and that what it secures is bringing the person forward. Ibn Qudama, a Hanbali jurist, says this guarantee is valid in the view of most scholars, and names Shurayh, Malik, al-Thawri, al-Layth and Abu Hanifa as holding it. A report that al-Shafi'i did not allow it is described as going against the stronger view of his own followers, who allow it. Ibn Qudama also holds that such a guarantee is not valid for a person who faces a fixed punishment, such as the penalty for theft.
rows.why: The aim was to make sure that a debtor would be present at a set place to pay his debt or fine, or to undergo a punishment.
accepted_by: the stronger view among the Shafi'is

rows.new_version_name: Joining liability in the claim (Hanafi) versus joining it in the obligation itself (majority)
rows.what_changed: The classical schools came to define kafala in two different ways. In the stronger Hanafi view, kafala joins one person's liability to another's in the claim for payment, without further limits. The majority, meaning the Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis, define it as joining the guarantor's liability to the debtor's in the duty to pay the right owed. A modern study gives the Hanafi definition as a joint obligation of guarantor and principal debtor in the claim of the debt only. The same study gives the Hanbali definition as a joint obligation of guarantor and guaranteed person in what the guaranteed party owes. It gives one Shafi'i jurist's definition as an undertaking to a right or debt that another party owes. A study of Malaysian banking sums up the split the same way: the Hanafis speak of a joint liability, while the other schools speak of joining the guarantor's liability to that of the person guaranteed.
rows.why: The schools differ over what the guarantor shares with the debtor: for the Hanafis it is the claim, and for the majority it is the obligation to pay the right owed.

rows.scholar: Imami (Shi'a) jurists, including 'Allama Hilli; restated today in the rulings of Ayatollah Sistani
rows.new_version_name: Daman as transfer of the debt, with kafala kept for producing a person (Imami)
rows.what_changed: In Imami jurisprudence, guarantee (daman) has traditionally been defined as a transfer of liability, called naql al-dhimma. On this view, the debt moves from the original debtor to the guarantor. A Shi'a reference work explains that in daman the debt passes to the guarantor, while in kafala it stays with the debtor. Kafala in this sense is a contract in which one party undertakes to bring a third person against whom the other party has a claim. The guarantor's only duty is to bring that person, and the beneficiary, called the makful lahu, may give up that right. The same work cites 'Allama Hilli, a Shi'a jurist, on a guarantor who promised to pay a sum if he failed to bring the person: he must do as he promised. Ayatollah Sistani's rulings on suretyship describe a form in which the guarantor takes the debtor's debt onto himself. Once that is done, the creditor cannot cancel the suretyship and go back to the original debtor.
rows.why: In these sources, daman moves the debt to the guarantor, while in kafala the debt stays with the debtor and the guarantor undertakes to bring a person against whom there is a claim.

rows.year_how_known: year the Ottoman civil code entered into force, as stated on Wikipedia
rows.scholar: Ottoman Mecelle commission headed by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha
rows.new_version_name: Guarantee as numbered law in the Ottoman civil code (Mecelle, Book III)
rows.what_changed: The Mecelle was the civil code of the Ottoman Empire in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. A commission headed by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha prepared it, issuing it in volumes from 1869 to 1876, and it came into force in 1877. Its content was based on the Hanafi legal tradition, which had official status in the empire. Its third book, on guarantee, defines a guarantee as adding one obligation to another in respect of a demand for a particular thing. It separates a personal guarantee, where someone becomes guarantor for another man in person, from a guarantee of property, where someone becomes guarantor for a payment. A personal guarantee is met by producing the person guaranteed. The code names the parties: the guarantor, the principal who is guaranteed, and the creditor in whose favour the guarantee is made. The person claiming under a guarantee may claim against the guarantor, and using his right against one party in no way ends his right to claim from the other.
rows.why: The code set out rules based on the Hanafi legal tradition in 1,851 articles and served as the civil code of the Ottoman Empire.
accepted_by: Hanafi (the legal tradition the code was based on)

rows.year_how_known: year of the ruling: 2nd session of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy, Jeddah, 22-28 December 1985
rows.scholar: International Islamic Fiqh Academy (OIC), Resolution No. 12 (12/2)
rows.new_version_name: Bank letter of guarantee with no fee beyond actual costs
rows.what_changed: Meeting in Jeddah in December 1985, the International Islamic Fiqh Academy issued a resolution on the letter of guarantee. It found that when a letter of guarantee has no cover, the issuer counts as having pledged jointly along with the third party, both for performance and for money. When the letter is covered, the tie between the client and the issuer is one of agency. The Academy ruled that no fee may be charged for issuing a letter of guarantee, whether it is covered or not. It allowed administrative charges for issuing either kind, as long as they do not go beyond the actual cost of similar services. Jordan's fatwa office later repeated this rule, citing the Academy's resolution, and said that charging actual expenses is allowed. It explained that a fee would turn the guarantee into a loan that brings a benefit, which is forbidden. It added that guarantee and loan are both done to please God, so taking payment for them is unlawful. In February 2023 the Academy took up letters of guarantee again, but put off a decision until more research was done.
rows.why: Some Islamic banks were taking a commission for letters of guarantee, while the ruling allows only administrative charges that do not exceed actual costs. The reasoning given is that a fee would turn the guarantee into a loan that brings a benefit.

rows.year_how_known: date of the ruling: 80th meeting of the Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia, 7 January 2009, as stated in a published study
rows.scholar: Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia; Al-Zuhayli cited for the need-based exception
rows.new_version_name: Guarantee for a fee (kafalah bil ujr) in Malaysian practice
rows.what_changed: A study notes that, classically, most Islamic jurists held it unlawful to charge a fee for a guarantee. The reason it gives is that kafala was a contract of tabarru', a free gift for which no reward is required. Citing Al-Zuhayli, the study says a fee is allowed only when there is a real need for the guarantee and the debtor cannot find a guarantor who does not charge. Malaysia's Islamic deposit insurance scheme, run by PIDM, uses kafala with a fee, called kafalah bil ujr. The scheme gives depositors takaful cover against losing their deposits if the bank cannot pay them back. The Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia approved this fee-based use of kafala at its 80th meeting on 7 January 2009. In Malaysian bank guarantees, known as BG-i, Islamic banks issue a letter of guarantee and undertake to meet the customer's obligation if the customer defaults.
rows.why: The study ties the fee to need: Al-Zuhayli allows it when no free guarantor can be found, and the deposit scheme uses it to protect depositors.

rows.new_version_name: Customary guarantee as a promise to make good losses (modern Imami thought and Iranian law)
rows.what_changed: A study of Imami jurisprudence and Iranian law notes that guarantee was traditionally defined as a transfer of liability. It describes a model of guarantee that is not based on transferring the debt, but on the guarantor's promise to make good losses. It argues that the older model no longer explains dealings such as bank guarantees, construction contracts, property insurance and credit arrangements. It credits Sayyid Yazdi with a pioneering role in accepting guarantees that go beyond strict debt transfer. It says that Mohaqiq Damad reshaped these ideas in his General Theory of Conditions and Obligations. A Shi'a reference work adds that under Iranian law, a guarantor who breaks the contract must pay for the damage that results.
rows.why: The study holds that in modern settings such as bank guarantees, the traditional model no longer gives an adequate explanation.

rows.new_version_name: Rahn: the pledge in hand named in Qur'an 2:283
rows.what_changed: The Qur'an says that if people are on a journey and no scribe can be found, a security can be taken. A commentary on the verse explains that the pledge is given to the creditor in place of writing the transaction down. The same verse says that where the two sides trust each other, no security is needed, but the borrower must honour that trust. Rahn is described as a financial contract between the person who gives the pledge and the person who receives it, in which an asset is pledged as collateral to the receiver. A commentary on the verse says that in a credit deal it is allowed to keep something as security for a debt. It adds that the holder's only right is to keep the item in his possession until the debt is paid. Muslim jurists agree that the pledge is allowed in general.
rows.why: The verse allows a security in place of a written record when people are on a journey and no scribe can be found.

Al-Bukhari's hadith collection places pledging in places with a settled population next to that verse. In one report, the Prophet bought food on credit for a limited period and pledged his armour for it. Another report says he pledged his armour for barley. A commentary on the verse adds that his shield was pledged with a Jewish man for thirty wasq, about 180 kg, of barley. rows.scholar: Hanbali jurists, following the hadith on the ridden and milked animal
rows.new_version_name: Use of the pledge in return for its upkeep (ridden and milked animals)
rows.what_changed: A hadith in al-Bukhari's collection says a pledged animal may be ridden because of what is spent on it, and its milk may be drunk on the same basis. Jurists split over whether the lender who holds a pledge may use it. The majority hold that the lender may not use the pledge at all, and that the owner must pay for what it needs. The Hanafis say the lender may not use the pledged item for service, riding, living in or wearing. For the Malikis, such use is not allowed when the debt comes from a loan, because it would be a loan that brings a benefit. The view that the benefit of the pledge belongs to the owner, who also bears its cost, is reported as the school of al-Shafi'i. The Hanbalis, with some early jurists, allow the lender to use the pledge in proportion to what he spends on it. They limit this to animals that are ridden or milked. For items that need no upkeep, such as a house or goods, the lender may not use them at all without the owner's permission. For land and similar property that needs no upkeep, the lender may not exploit it, because the deal would become a loan with interest, which is riba itself.
rows.why: The hadith tied the benefit of a pledged animal to the cost of keeping it. Some jurists held that a lender's benefit from a pledge given for a loan would be riba.
rejected_by: Maliki (when the debt is a loan)

rows.scholar: Ottoman Mecelle commission headed by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha
rows.new_version_name: Codified pledge law in the Ottoman Mecelle (Majalla)
rows.what_changed: The Mecelle was the civil code of the Ottoman Empire in the late 19th and early 20th century, and it set out rules for the pledge. It is described as the first codification of Sharia law by an Islamic nation, and its content follows the Hanafi tradition. It was issued in sixteen volumes between 1869 and 1876 and came into force in 1877. The code defines a pledge as setting aside property from which a claim can be paid. The contract is made by offer and acceptance, but it stays incomplete and can be withdrawn until the lender actually takes possession. The lender may not use the pledge without the owner's permission. The lender pays to keep the pledge safe, such as the rent of the place and a watchman's wages, while the owner pays for an animal's feed and keeper. If the owner refuses to pay when the debt falls due, the court orders him to sell the pledge, and if he still refuses, the court sells it.
rows.why: A commission headed by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha prepared it as the civil code of the Ottoman Empire, drawing its content from the Hanafi tradition.
