rows.year_how_known: year the first Islamic pawnshop began its services (January 1992), as the page states
rows.scholar: Muassasah Gadaian Islam Terengganu (set up by the Terengganu Religious and Malay Custom Council)
rows.new_version_name: Ar-Rahnu: Islamic pawnbroking in Malaysia
rows.what_changed: Ar-rahnu, whose name comes from the Arabic word rahn, works as Islamic microcredit. It was first mentioned in a speech written by Jaffar bin Hussein, then governor of Bank Negara Malaysia, and given at Universiti Sains Malaysia on 9 March 1990. The Terengganu Islamic Pawnshop Corporation, set up by the state's religious council, began offering Islamic pawnbroking in January 1992. Permodalan Kelantan Berhad also introduced the service in March 1992. In August 1993 the finance minister announced that Bank Rakyat, working with a national Islamic development foundation, would offer the scheme to the public. Bank Islam Malaysia, the country's first Islamic bank, brought it to its Kelantan branch in 1998. The scheme combines several contracts: a loan (qard), the pledge (rahn), safekeeping (wadi'ah) and a fee (ujrah). The fee is charged as payment for keeping the item safe, and the institutions do not charge interest. At first the scheme fell under the 1972 Pawnshop Act, but it is now exempt from that Act.
rows.why: It was introduced as an alternative to ordinary pawnbroking for Muslims. Ordinary pawnshops can charge between 14 and 24 percent interest a year.

rows.scholar: Dewan Syariah Nasional - Majelis Ulama Indonesia (National Sharia Board of the Indonesian Ulema Council)
rows.new_version_name: Rahn under Indonesia's national sharia ruling (sharia pawnshops)
rows.what_changed: In June 2002 Indonesia's National Sharia Board ruled that a loan secured by pledging goods as rahn is allowed, under set conditions. The lender may hold the pledged item until all of the debt is paid. In principle the lender may not use the item unless the owner allows it, and then only without lowering its value and only to cover its upkeep. Upkeep and storage are the owner's duty and cost, even when the lender does the work. The storage fee may not be set by the size of the loan. If the owner still cannot pay, the item is sold by auction in line with Islamic law; any surplus goes back to the owner and any shortfall stays his debt. Another ruling, number 26, allows gold to be pledged on the principle of rahn. The cost of storing the pledged goods is set on the basis of a rental (ijarah) contract. A later study argues that the two rulings mainly justify the existing financial system rather than serving the need for Islamic-law compliance. It also finds practice that departs from the ruling, such as merging the rental contract with the pledge and running the pledge through a loan contract. It warns that taking profit on the loan through upkeep or storage charges would be riba.
rows.why: The ruling allows a loan backed by a pledge, but only under set conditions. It bars tying the storage fee to the loan size, and critics note that profit taken on a loan through such charges would count as riba.

rows.new_version_name: Rahn as collateral in Islamic bank financing
rows.what_changed: Islamic financial institutions in Malaysia use rahn, and its use varies from bank to bank: some banks use it in home financing, car financing and long-term financing. The house or the car is pledged to guarantee that the amount financed is repaid. One bank accepts all types of collateral, including property, fixed deposits and shares. The study describes rahn as a contract in which an asset is pledged to assure that the pledgor's obligation will be met. In one arrangement, the customer keeps gold with the bank under the principle of wadiah yad dhamanah and pays ujrah, the bank grants a loan (qard), and the customer pledges the gold. The study sees a problem in requiring the deposited item to be pledged while also charging for its safekeeping. It concludes that rahn in these institutions meets its purpose, but that some transactions using it need review to comply with Islamic law.
rows.why: The pledge guarantees that the amount financed will be repaid.

rows.what_changed: The Qur'an asks who will lend to God a good loan that God will multiply many times over. The same verse adds that God alone decreases and increases wealth, and that all people will return to Him. One commentary reads the verse as God urging His servants to spend in His cause. Another commentary says the verse was revealed about a man of the Ansar, the Helpers, named Abu'l-Dahdah. A further commentary explains that the word "loan" here stands for good deeds and for spending in the way of God. It adds that the word is a figure of speech, since everything already belongs to God.

rows.year_how_known: death year of Ibn al-Mundhir (d. 318/930), who reported the consensus
rows.scholar: Ibn al-Mundhir (reporting the consensus of jurists)
rows.new_version_name: Classical qard: a free loan where any agreed extra is usury
rows.what_changed: The jurists set one firm rule for the loan: the lender may not make any extra a condition. Ibn al-Mundhir, who died in 930, reported that scholars agreed that if a lender makes an increase or a gift a condition and lends on that basis, taking the increase is riba, or usury. A modern study states that all the juristic schools agree it is forbidden to put a condition in the loan that the borrower must return more than he received. It makes no difference whether the extra is large or small. The reason given is that such a benefit goes against the free, gratuitous nature of the loan. One statement of this consensus puts it sharply: any stipulated increase is usury, even a handful of animal fodder or a single grain. A saying that any loan which brings a benefit to the lender is usury is also reported, but its chain of narrators is questioned. Even so, scholars accepted its meaning and it became a legal maxim.
rows.why: The loan was meant to be gratuitous, so any increase or gift made a condition for the lender was treated as usury.

rows.scholar: Trade practice (merchants and public treasuries); debated by the jurists
rows.new_version_name: Suftaja: a loan repaid in another town (bill of exchange)
rows.what_changed: The suftaja was a loan in which the lender sets another place for repayment; such an instrument was commonly used to lessen the dangers of travel. In the Abbasid period it was used for payments from local treasuries to the central treasury and to merchants. Its legal standing was disputed: some jurists treated it as a loan, while others saw it as a different kind of arrangement. Some jurists said that a condition to repay a loan in another place benefits the lender and is therefore forbidden. Others said such a condition is valid as long as it causes the borrower no inconvenience and carries no risk. Ahmad, the founder of the Hanbali school, is reported to have said it is not allowed in a loan, but also to have allowed it because it benefits both sides. Ibn Qudamah, a Hanbali scholar, judged the correct view to be that it is allowed, since both parties gain and neither is harmed. Other jurists viewed this condition as strongly disliked, to the point of being forbidden. A modern study asserts that all bank transfers and remittances are forms of the bill of exchange.
rows.why: The bill of exchange was meant to make trade easier and lighten burdens. Without it, a debtor had to send the money owed all the way to the creditor's country.
accepted_by: Ibn Qudamah (Hanbali), if it harms neither party

rows.what_changed: In 1983 Iran established its Usury-Free Banking Act, and its Monetary and Banking Act was amended. Under that law, one of the main objectives of the Iranian banking system was to create the facilities needed to extend gharz-al-hasaneh, described as interest-free consumer loans. For some deposits, the relationship between the depositor and the bank is based on lending and borrowing that bears no interest. One type, the gharz-al-hasaneh current account, is like a checking account in the conventional banking system. Money placed in gharz-al-hasaneh savings accounts is used by banks to extend interest-free consumer loans.
rows.why: One of the main objectives set under the usury-free banking law was to create the facilities needed for interest-free consumer loans.

rows.what_changed: In October 1986 the International Islamic Fiqh Academy, meeting in Amman, Jordan, answered questions put to it by the Islamic Development Bank. It ruled that a loan-related fee may be charged, but only within the limit of the actual expenses. Any fee above the real cost of the service is forbidden, because it counts as riba, or usury.
rows.why: Questions from the Islamic Development Bank led to a ruling that allowed the real costs of running a loan to be charged, but treated anything beyond them as usury.

rows.year_how_known: year of the ruling (9th session, Abu Dhabi, 1–6 April 1995), as the page states
rows.scholar: International Islamic Fiqh Academy (Organization of the Islamic Conference), Resolution No. 86 (3/9)
rows.new_version_name: Current account as qard: the customer lends to the bank
rows.what_changed: In April 1995 the International Islamic Fiqh Academy met in Abu Dhabi and ruled on ordinary bank deposits. It held that money in current accounts, whether at Islamic banks or interest-based banks, is in Islamic law a loan from the customer to the bank. The reason given is that the bank is answerable for keeping this money safe and is bound to pay it back whenever the customer asks. Whether the bank is financially strong or weak does not change this ruling. The duty to guarantee these accounts falls on the bank's shareholders, as the borrowers. Customers who hold investment accounts are not asked to share in guaranteeing the current accounts.
rows.why: The bank receiving current-account deposits is answerable for their safety and bound to return them on call, so the Academy classed these deposits as loans.

rows.scholar: Akhuwat Foundation (founded by Muhammad Amjad Saqib)
rows.new_version_name: Qard hasan microfinance (Qarz-e-Hasna)
rows.what_changed: In 2001 Muhammad Amjad Saqib founded Akhuwat in Pakistan, starting with a first few interest-free loans. Akhuwat is a nonprofit that provides interest-free microfinance to people without access to formal financial services. It has given out 4.5 million such loans, which it calls Qarz-e-Hasna. Places of worship, including local mosques, churches and temples, serve as centres for handing out the loans and for community involvement. Borrowers may choose to give money back to the programme as a donation, but this is optional.
rows.why: The aim is to reach people who are shut out of formal financial services.

rows.year_how_known: year of the ruling (23rd session, Medina, 28 October–1 November 2018), as the page states
rows.scholar: International Islamic Fiqh Academy (Organization of Islamic Cooperation), Resolution No. 222 (6/23)
rows.new_version_name: Current-account qard: which bank perks are allowed
rows.what_changed: In 2018 the International Islamic Fiqh Academy, meeting in Medina, ruled on the perks banks give to current account holders. It repeated that current accounts, at Islamic or interest-based banks, are loans in Islamic law. Material extras added because of the money held in the account, similar to prizes for taking a loan such as flight tickets or electronic devices, are forbidden. Such arrangements are forbidden because they amount to a loan that brings the lender a benefit. Non-material services, such as priority service at branches, regular account statements and international ATM cards, are allowed. Some advantages may be counted as advertising and marketing costs, as long as they are not linked to the loan, its amount or its length.
rows.why: The ruling held that material extras tied to current-account money are forbidden because they make the deposit a loan that brings a benefit.
